messages.body_plain:
Hello Christy,

I have succesfully used the GPSA method to compare pelvic shape between anuran species. The work was previously embargoed on bioRxiv, but you can now access it in Chapter 5 of my doctoral thesis (https://www.tdx.cat/handle/10803/666609). The only difference with your samples is that my models were extracted from CTscans of preserved specimens, so I had no missing data. Nonetheless, if you want to talk with me about my experience using GPSA for this analysis please feel free to contact me offlist.

Best wishes,
Javier H. Santos-Santos

From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> on behalf of Christy Hipsley <christy...@unimelb.edu.au>
Sent: Thursday, February 27, 2020 04:27
To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: [geomorph-r-package] shape analyses to compare partial fossils to complete modern specimens

Dear Geomorphers (& apologies for the cross-post if you're also on Morphmet),

I'm seeking advice on how to approach a dataset of ~400 microCT scans of fossil frog ilia (hip bones) that are preserved with varying completeness along the ilial shaft, meaning that some are broken off shorter than others.

Otherwise they are fairly simple structures with an elongate tubular shaft that articulates with the sacrum anteriorly, and a partial socket on the other end that articulates with the pubis and ischium posteriorly to hold the femoral head in a ball&socket joint. I include a screenshot here of a surface model of a right ilium in lateral view, segmented from a CT scan of a complete ethanol-preserved frog (left), and 3 fossil ilia (right) it to illustrate the degree of variation in shaft length caused by preservation.

I'm considering a few 3D approaches to analyse the fossils together with whole body scans of modern frogs, and I would appreciate some feedback regarding how to deal with breakage/missing data. These are, but not limited to:

anatomically-defined and sliding semi-landmarks
high density point cloud comparison, or GPSA (Pomidor et al. 2016 <https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0150368>)
pseudolandmarks in auto3dgm (Boyer et al. 2015 <https://anatomypubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ar.23084>)
For extant frogs I prefer to work with the whole skeleton (either in the volume or as a surface mesh), because the ilium is not always possible to cleanly isolate from adjacent bones. Checkpoint Stratovan seems a good solution for landmarking since it can take both formats, but I'm still stuck with the issue of how to compare broken fossils. I've thought of working backwards with the extant specimens - first landmarking the entire structure and then systematically deleting points along the shaft to see if/when the signal is lost. But I'm not sure if one can delete points from patches or curves, if I would use those to describe the shaft. I don't believe that estimating missing landmarks would be appropriate in this case.

Apologies for the long post, but I would really appreciate any ideas on how to proceed.

Best,

Christy

University of Melbourne / Museums Victoria

messages.body_plain:
Jessica,

Have you used picknplot.shape?  It allows you to make deformation grids for any point in the plot.

Also, plot.two.b.pls is an S3 generic plot function, meaning you can add stuff to your plot, just like any general R plot.  For example,

PLS <- two.b.pls(shape, mydata, …)
P <- plot(PLS, pch = 19, col = “yellow”)
text(x, y, mylabels, ...)

where mylabels is a vector of labels and x, y, are the coordinates where you want the labels to go.  You can find these in the P$plot.args, if they are the same locations as points.  Then, of course,

picknplot.shape(P, ...)

will allow you to generate deformation grids, if the data you used in PLS is appropriate (3D array rather than a matrix).

Good luck!
Mike

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] curious modularity result
messages.body_plain:
Dave,

The ‘curious’ finding is because your data are more highly integrated than they are modular.

First, I ran your code. The method is doing what is expected: it is comparing the observed CR to the permuted values, and the percentage of permuted lower than the observed provides the significance value. So the math is correct.  And following standard procedure one would interpret this has having greater modularity than expected by a random association of landmarks to modules.

However, you are correct that the observed value is greater than 1.0, as are most of the permuted values in the histogram distribution. This implies relatively greater variation between modules than within them: a hint that there may be strong integration. And in fact, running your data through a PLS finds crazy-high integration between the 2 modules:

integration.test(CAP23.gpa$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp> = CAP23.gps)

r-PLS: 0.957

P-value: 0.001

Effect Size: 12.7157

Look at that effect size: 12.7!  That is super-strong integration in this system. The two modules (halves of the arrowhead as it turns out) covary in a near-perfect manner.

Please recall our earlier thread on this topic (on this googlegroup) where it was stated that modularity and integration are not mutually exclusive: nor are they either-or options. One can have significant integration between modules who are themselves significantly modular. In the case of your data, I conjecture that the integration signal is considerably stronger than is the modular one: a conjecture born out by comparison of effect sizes (12.7 vs. 3.05).

Dean

messages.subject: Identifying points on PCA graph
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am still getting used to R so forgive me if there is an easy solution. I have one specimen that is skewing my results on my PCA graph so want to find a way to identify what specimen it is so that I can resolve this.
Here is my code:

library(geomorph)
mydata <- readland.tps("Flipper ratios NEW.TPS", specID = "ID")
classifier <- read.csv("classifier flipper ratios.csv", header = TRUE)
is.factor(classifier$Morphotype)
coords <- as.matrix(mydata)
flipperratios.gpa <- gpagen(mydata, print.progress = FALSE)
summary(flipperratios.gpa)
plotAllSpecimens(flipperratios.gpa$coords, mean = TRUE, links = NULL, label = TRUE, plot.param = list())
flipperratios.pca <-plotTangentSpace(flipperratios.gpa$coords, axis1 = 1, axis2 = 2, groups = classifier$Morphotype, legend = TRUE)

Hope you can help, thanks in advance!

In your particular your outlier is has the maximum value along PC1, so convenient R function for that would be
which.max(flipperratios.pca$pcscores$PC1) (or whatever the vector holding the PC1 scores)

You can also use identify() function to get the actual value of a point you click on the graph

alternatively you can try to plot the labels of the specimens on top of PC values.

For a more general solution, where you want to be able to scroll over any point in a plot and see its identifier, have a look at qtlcharts.

The plots here include several nice examples: https://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/do_diagnostics.html

Here's a link to the package page: https://kbroman.org/qtlcharts/

And here's some very simple example code (assumed you've successfully installed all packages)
library(qtlcharts)
mymax <- 100
x <- 1:mymax
y <- sqrt(1:mymax)
labs <- paste0("ID", 1:mymax)
iplot(x, y, indID=labs,
      chartOpts=list(xlab="Integer", ylab="Sqrt"))

David
